actions they have taken (or not taken) to stabilise the financial system and wider
economy since crisis broke in 2007. For every paean of praise for their innovations
in injecting liquidity, keeping markets open and supporting macroeconomic
recovery, there is a chorus of reproof censuring central banks for breaching a crucial
boundary between central banking and fiscal policy. Those criticisms are essentially
about political economy, and as such amount to an important challenge to the
legitimacy of today’s central banks. 2
The terrain – and the object of the criticisms – covers three separable but linked
areas: monetary policy, lender of last resort, and what has become known as “credit
policy”. My focus here is lender of last resort (LOLR), where especially in the United
States the atmosphere is probably most toxic, poisoning debates about central
banking more generally. Once central banks are perceived as having overstepped
the mark in bailing out bust institutions, critics look for overreach in their more
overtly macroeconomic interventions too. That, more or less, is what has happened
in the United States.3
The relative neglect of LOLR in the core literature on central banking over the
past twenty years is a tragedy – one that contributed to central banks losing their
way and finding themselves struggling for breath when faced with a liquidity crisis
in 2007. That mainstream macroeconomics devoted so much effort to
conceptualising the case for central bank independence and to articulating ever
more sophisticated models of how monetary policy works while leaving out of those
models the fragile banking system that called central banking into existence as a
liquidity insurer in the first place warrants careful explanation – most probably by
political scientists, sociologists and historians of ideas.
Of course, there wasn’t complete silence on LOLR. The technical academic
literature advanced,4 but was largely separate from policy debates, no doubt
because LOLR was widely regarded as a relic of the past. With a few exceptions,
prior to the crisis policy-oriented commentary was dominated, especially in the
United States, by arguments for limiting or abolishing liquidity insurance and,
indeed, central banking itself. 5 As such, rightly or wrongly, those who remained engaged with LOLR, including within the Federal Reserve system, are often
perceived to be politically partisan and, as such, pursuing a sectional interest.
Nevertheless, that does not make a case for casting them and their arguments
aside. Both they and events themselves have raised serious questions and
challenges.
The most serious accusation from critics is that (some) central banks aided
insolvent firms, and stretched beyond their legal authority to do so.6 The most
serious practical challenge seen by central bankers themselves is that firms have
become deeply reluctant to turn to the LOLR, especially via bilateral facilities such as
the Discount Window, due to the stigma involved, leaving the financial system
fragile in ways it is hard for regulation to undo. These sound like quite different
problems. But I shall argue that they are closely linked, and outline a cure.
Only slightly less momentous are a host of questions brought to the fore by the
2007–09 phase of the crisis: should central banks lend against a wide or narrow
class of collateral; should they provide liquidity assistance to non-banks; should they
act as market-makers of last resort; what happens when the liquidity shortage is in
foreign currency? Each issue presents distinct technical and governance challenges.
None of them is covered by Bagehot, who needs updating if only for that reason.
After addressing them in sequence, I will bring things together with some broader
thoughts on the governance and democratic accountability of central banks in the
area of liquidity insurance.
The underlying theme is legitimacy: how to ensure that the central banks’ role
of LOLR is legitimate in democratic societies where powers and responsibilities have
in effect been delegated by the elected legislature. As a general matter, I have
argued elsewhere that a regime for delegating powers to an independent agency
needs to satisfy four design principles or precepts: high-level purposes, goals and
powers need to be framed in primary legislation, or fleshed out by government
under statutory authority; central banks need to operate within that domain
according to reasonably clear principles; transparency needs to be sufficient, if only
with a lag, for both the regime and the central bank’s stewardship of it to be
monitored and debated by the public and, crucially, the legislature; and there needs
to be clarity about what happens, substantively and procedurally, during a crisis
and, in particular, when a central bank reaches the boundary of its authority.7 What
those design precepts entail in practice depends, of course, on the substance and
purpose of the regime. Here the question is the LOLR function.
Four concepts shape the analysis of the LOLR: time consistency, moral hazard,
adverse selection, and what I call the “fiscal carve-out” delineating the space in
which an independent central bank can operate. How those concepts are handled
shapes a jurisdiction’s regime. A brief word on each is warranted.
Acting as the lender of last resort involves making commitments: to lend in
order to stave off or contain systemic distress. Those commitments need to be
credible, which requires amongst other things that they be time consistent. The
regime won’t work well if people believe a central bank will change its mind, or has
no clear principles. As with any kind of insurance, liquidity insurance creates incentives to take
more of the insured risk, in this case liquidity risk. Moral hazard is a major issue that
must be addressed if a regime is to serve society well over time. Unless care is
taken, that can conflict with time consistency. If a central bank pledges not to
provide assistance in some form or other (eg to insolvent firms) but then buckles in
the face of systemic distress, future promises to the same end will probably not be
believed, exacerbating moral hazard and putting the financial system on an unstable
course. So ways have to be found to underpin the credibility of commitments
designed to contain moral hazard.
Many types of insurance are plagued by a problem of adverse selection, with
only the riskiest being prepared to take up the offer of insurance. That leaves the
insurer exposed to bad risks. In the case of LOLR, which serves a public policy
purpose, the consequential challenge is how to design a regime that firms are
prepared to use before it is too late to contain the liquidity crisis and its wider costs
to society.
Finally, there is no getting away from the fact that LOLR assistance is risky.
However well protected, the central bank can in principle suffer losses. This isn’t a
theoretical point: losses have crystallised in practice. In the first instance, the central
bank will cover its losses by drawing on its capital or by paying less seigniorage over
to the government. Either way, that simply transfers the costs to government.
Ultimately, losses are a fiscal issue. They must be covered by higher taxation (or
lower public spending) or by higher seigniorage, ie resorting to inflation as a tax.
The LOLR regime therefore needs to be framed by a broader fiscal carve-out defined
for each jurisdiction’s central bank. In most countries, this fiscal carve-out (FCO) is
implicit or scattered across many statutes and agreements. It is my contention,
articulated more fully elsewhere, that the FCO should be explicit, as complete as
possible, and transparent.8
Those four concepts run through this analysis. But first, what is the LOLR, and
why does it exist?

The critics say that, once central banks are perceived as having overstepped the mark in bailing out bust institutions, people look for overreach in their more overtly macroeconomic interventions as well; which is what has already happened in the US.

Can you relate the following to any major ideas in the world of philosophy?

The history of the colour blue is quite fascinating, as it was not as commonly mentioned or referred to in early literature and art as other colours, such as red, yellow, or green. Specialists believe that this could be due to the fact that blue is not a colour that appears frequently in nature, especially as a pigment or material that could be used for painting or dyeing.

The lack of blue in ancient literature is notably exemplified by the absence of the colour from the works of Homer, the ancient Greek poet who wrote the Iliad and the Odyssey. In these epic poems, different colours like black, white, and red are mentioned, but the colour blue is entirely absent. It is not just that the word blue is missing in these works, but also that the descriptions involving colours or shades are never linked to anything that resembles blue.

Similarly, the ancient Hebrew Bible hardly mentions the colour blue, and ancient Egyptian texts from thousands of years ago also seem to skip this colour in their descriptions. Blue pigments for dyes and paints were often expensive and difficult to produce in those times. Consequently, the artists and writers of the time were not exposed to this colour as frequently as we are today.

This absence of the colour blue in early literature raises a fascinating question about the relationship between language and perception: if there is no name for something, does it truly exist for those who have no vocabulary to describe it? According to the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, the structure of a language determines or greatly influences its speakers’ worldview. If a culture does not have a specific word for a colour, their perception of that colour may be significantly influenced or limited as a result.

Apart from blue, there are other instances in history where the absence of a term or label affected perceptions. For instance, some indigenous cultures categorize colours differently, grouping certain shades that Western societies might consider distinct under a single term. Language and colour perception can have serious implications for how different cultures perceive the world and can even lead to social divisions or misunderstandings.

The well-known example of the Inuit people and their various words for snow is another significant demonstration of this phenomenon. Supposedly, they have dozens (some sources claim even up to 50) of words to describe different types of snow and ice, which highlights how important these distinctions are for their survival and way of life. Comparatively, for people living in warmer climates where the snow rarely falls, a detailed vocabulary for describing snow is not necessary.

The history of the colour blue and its lack of reference in early literature is an intriguing example of how language can shape perception and help us understand the complex relationship between words and the world around us. With different cultures having unique language systems, our perception of colour, nature, and many other aspects of life can be significantly influenced by our words, leading to diverse and rich understandings of the world.

The fascinating history of the colour blue and its absence in early literature can be related to various ideas in the world of philosophy. One significant idea that comes to light from this history is the relationship between language and perception. The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, which posits that the structure of a language influences its speakers' worldview, can be linked to this discussion. The absence of the colour blue in early literary works raises the question of whether something exists for those who have no vocabulary to describe it, which highlights the impact of language on perception.

Another philosophical idea that emerges from this example is the cultural relativism of language and perception. As different cultures have unique language systems that categorize colours and other aspects of life differently, it underlines the idea that our understanding of reality is profoundly influenced by the cultural context in which we live. This can lead to diverse and rich perspectives on the world, but can also cause social divisions or misunderstandings when differing cultural perceptions collide.

The history of the colour blue also reminds us of the importance of language in shaping our experiences and understanding of the world. It highlights the power and limitations of our vocabulary and serves as an example of how even seemingly fundamental aspects of our lives, like colours, can be influenced by the language we speak and the words we have at our disposal.
can you elaborate on this further, using more recent philosophers, and citing sources, APA style?

The history of the color blue and its absence in early literature provides an interesting connection to recent philosophical discussions around language and perception. One scholar whose work has significant bearing on this topic is Ludwig Wittgenstein, a 20th-century philosopher known for his philosophical investigations into language. Wittgenstein's concept of language-games, which he argued form the basis of our understanding of the world, emphasizes the integral role language plays in shaping human experiences (Wittgenstein, 1953).

In relation to the example of the color blue, Wittgenstein's work suggests that language not only dictates the way we categorize and perceive color, but also highlights the importance of a shared understanding and use of language within a cultural context for effective communication (Wittgenstein, 1953). Without a specific word or concept for the color blue, it would be difficult for an individual or group of people within a society to accurately perceive or discuss the color.

More recent linguistic and cognitive research also supports the relationship between language and perception. One influential theory is the linguistic relativity hypothesis, also known as the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, which posits that the structure of a language can influence or determine an individual's thoughts, experiences, and perceptions (Whorf, 1956). This hypothesis has been the subject of ongoing debate and research, with various studies examining the impact of language on color perception, spatial cognition, and other aspects of human experience (Gumperz & Levinson, 1996).

In a study by Kay and Kempton (1984), researchers found that the language one speaks can influence the way they categorize and differentiate colors, supporting the idea that language can shape perception. In a different context, research on the indigenous Himba tribe in Namibia demonstrated that their unique linguistic categorization of colors affected their ability to discriminate between certain shades of green and blue (Roberson, Davidoff, Davies, & Shapiro, 2005).

The history of the color blue and its lack of reference in early literature reinforces the importance of language in shaping perception. It highlights that our perception of color, nature, and other aspects of life can be significantly influenced by the available words and language systems within our culture.

References:

Gumperz, J. J., & Levinson, S. C. (Eds.). (1996). _Rethinking Linguistic Relativity_. Cambridge University Press.

Kay, P., & Kempton, W. (1984). What is the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis? _American Anthropologist, 86_(1), 65–79.

Roberson, D., Davidoff, J., Davies, I., & Shapiro, L. R. (2005). Color categories: Evidence for the cultural relativity hypothesis. _Cognitive Psychology, 50_(4), 378–411.

Whorf, B. L. (1956). _Language, thought, and reality: Selected writings of Benjamin Lee Whorf_. MIT Press.

Wittgenstein, L. (1953). _Philosophical investigations_. Basil Blackwell.

The concept of the relationship between language and perception, as observed through the history of the color blue, can indeed be examined through the lens of the philosophical idea of 'being vs. becoming.' 'Being' refers to the idea that something exists in a fixed and unchangeable state, whereas 'becoming' represents the notion that everything in the world is in a constant state of change and flux. This philosophical dichotomy dates back to ancient Greek philosophers like Parmenides (who emphasized 'being') and Heraclitus (who focused on 'becoming').

When discussing the color blue and its absence in early literature, we can consider 'being' as an intrinsic quality of the color itself, irrespective of the language used to describe it. In this view, blue exists as a fundamental aspect of reality, whether or not a particular linguistic or cultural group has a term for it.

In contrast, the 'becoming' perspective emphasizes the dynamic and evolving nature of human perception and understanding. From this viewpoint, the concept of blue as a distinct color emerges through cultural, linguistic, and historical processes. As people gain access to new pigments, develop new technologies for creating and reproducing colors, or encounter different cultural perspectives on color, the notion of blue transforms and evolves over time.

Examining the history of the color blue through the lens of 'being vs. becoming' illustrates how the perception of color can span both perspectives. While the physical reality of blue might exist independently of human language ('being'), our understanding, appreciation, and experience of it are shaped by cultural and linguistic factors that change over time ('becoming'). This also emphasizes the significance of understanding the complex relationship between language, culture, and our perception of reality—a relationship that reflects the ongoing interplay between the ideas of 'being' and 'becoming' in human experience.

Every body paragraph should link back to this prompt and the thesis as well. First make an intro that talks about MIlans history with the drug and the 2016 problems. Here is the data: Each year about 3.6 million Americans are prescribed EpiPen, the epinephrine auto-injector. The EpiPen is a life-saving treatment for anaphylactic reactions, which are caused by allergens such as nuts, seafood, and insect bites. A sharp increase in EpiPen’s price between 2009 and 2016 caused outrage, and prompted debate over whether Mylan N.V, the owner of EpiPen, acted unethically. Beyond the behaviour of Mylan, EpiPen’s price increases raise questions about the conditions of the US pharmaceutical market, and whether existing regulations and laws are sufficient to protect consumers.

Epipen Price Increases 
In 2007, Mylan N.V. acquired the right to market EpiPen as part of its acquisition of Merck KgaA. In 2009, Mylan began to steadily increase the price of EpiPen. In 2009, the wholesale price (the price which pharmacies paid) was $103.50 for a two-pack of autoinjectors. By July 2013 the price was up to $264.50, and it rose a further 75 percent to $461 by May of 2015. By May of 2016, the price rose again up to $608.61. Over a seven year period, the price of EpiPen had risen about 500% in total.
In the summer of 2016, the Mylan EpiPen pricing crisis broke into public consciousness and for months
dominated public discourse about the importance of governance, transparency and ethics in business and society. It
brought a renewed focus on corporate governance, the system of checks and balances that seeks to make corporate
boards and management accountable and ensure that they operate in the interest of their stakeholders (Ragas & Culp,
2014). The crisis also brought attention to the potential impact of governance on stakeholders of public corporations and
challenged Mylan to defend its corporate governance principles. Known for its leadership in the global generics and
specialty pharma sector, Mylan N.V. is a pharmaceutical company that prides itself on its vision of setting new standards in
health, improving access to life-saving medications and maintaining an enduring commitment to excellence in corporate
governance (Mylan.com, 2015).
In 2007, Mylan acquired the EpiPen, a medical device that is used to treat anaphylactic shock or life-threatening
allergic reactions (Czarneki, 2016). After the acquisition, the company became known for its marketing drive to create
awareness about the dangers of allergic reactions and for its lobbying efforts to make the EpiPen available in every home
and school. However, in August 2016, Mylan came under public scrutiny after users of the EpiPen and their families began
to speak up about the constantly rising price of the life-saving drug. Between 2007 and 2016 the price of a 2-pack EpiPen
rose from $100 to over $600 (Ramsey, 2016). Executive compensation at Mylan also rose, with the salary of Heather
Bresch, its CEO, rising by 670% to $18.9 million in 2015 (Maremont, 2016).
The situation led to a congressional hearing and the company’s CEO, Heather Bresch, was invited to present the
position of her company on the price increases. In response, Mylan maintained its stance on the fairness of the price
increases but announced that it would offer a generic version of the EpiPen at $300 per pen and give a discount to families
who cannot afford the drug based on their family income levels (Bomey, 2016). Meanwhile, the EpiPen crisis and the
resultant Congressional hearing had already put a searchlight on Mylan’s corporate governance standards, especially in
relation to fair pricing, transparency, disclosure, fair competition, executive compensation and generally acceptable
accounting principles. So how well did Mylan fare in keeping its corporate decisions in alignment with its corporate
governance policy? The following case study analyzes the important role of corporate governance in sustaining trust,
credibility, accountability, and profitability for Mylan and its potential effects on the company’s relationship with its various
stakeholders.
1.1 | Company History with EpiPen
Mylan was established in 1961, when two US Army colleagues, Milan “Mike” Puskar and Don Panoz decided to
start selling medical supplies to doctors and pharmacists from the back of a Pontiac car in White Sulfur Springs, Virginia.
From those humble beginnings, Mylan has come a long way. Today, it is a leader in the global generics and specialty
3
pharmaceutical sector with sales operations in over 165 countries and territories. Originally known as Milan, the company
grew to become a global player with a 35,000-strong workforce that strives to provide access to high quality medicine to
over 7 billion people across the globe (Mylan.com, 2015). It has 39 manufacturing facilities in 10 countries and offers
several name brand medications as well as over 1,400 generic pharmaceuticals (Mylan.com, 2015).
One of Mylan’s most recognized specialty products is the EpiPen (epinephrine injection, USP), an auto-injector
which is used in cases of emergency life-threatening allergic reactions or anaphylaxis. The device was first invented for
use by the military, EpiPen was first approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 1987 (Ramsey, 2016). After
multiple change of hands, it was acquired by Mylan in 2007 from Merck KGaA. At the time, the EpiPen logged $200 million
in revenue (Koons & Langreth, 2015). When new federal guidelines were set in place in 2010, Mylan stopped the sales of
single pens and switched to twin-packs. Up to that point, 35% of patients were prescribed single EpiPens. The U.S. FDA
also changed the label rules so that EpiPen could be marketed to anyone at risk of an anaphylaxis reaction, rather than
just those with a history of it. This was a major benefit to those at risk and is also was an easy method for Mylan to get the
word out about the EpiPen.
1.2 | Mylan’s Mission, Vision and CSR Stance
In its mission statement, Mylan emphasizes its commitment to setting new standards in healthcare, social
responsibility, service excellence, improved access to medicines and global leadership in innovation. It states, “Doing
what's right is sacred to us. We behave responsibly, even when nobody's looking. We set high standards from which we
never back down. This uncompromising ethical stance helps to keep our products pure, our workers safe and the
environment clean” (Mylan.com, 2015). Speaking about Mylan’s corporate social responsibility (CSR), its CEO, Heather
Bresch said, “We weigh every decision we make with the utmost care, asking ourselves how it might affect all of our
stakeholders, including patients, customers, employees, communities, vendors, creditors and investors. Indeed, chances
are that you, or someone you care about, has a stake in Mylan’s success” (Mylan, 2015a).
According to its CSR report, Mylan says it performs audits to ensure that its governance processes are in line
with the company’s policies, laws and regulations, and it evaluates the implementation and maintenance of such policies
while looking for opportunities for improvement. Mylan has several programs set in place for monitoring business activity.
Mylan routes all contracts dealing with healthcare providers and government officials to its Office of Global Compliance
(OGC) and legal department to conduct due diligence on behalf of the parties involved (Mylan, 2015b). It provides vendors
that “may interact with government officials on [their] behalf with anti-corruption training. Since 2007, Mylan employees and
third parties have completed more than 20,000 anti-corruption training sessions” (Mylan, 2015a, p. 11, para 4).

### Essay on the Ethical and Economic Adequacy of EpiPen Pricing

#### Introduction

Mylan N.V.'s journey with the EpiPen has been fraught with controversy, marked by a dramatic turn in public perception from pharmaceutical innovator to symbol of corporate greed. This essay scrutinizes the extent to which the pricing practices of Mylan regarding the EpiPen have been ethically and economically justified. In 2007, the once modest pharmaceutical company Mylan acquired the rights to market the EpiPen from Merck KgaA, a move that deeply impacted the accessibility of life-saving treatment for millions suffering from severe allergic reactions. Fast forward to 2016, and the ballooning cost of EpiPens raised a tempest of discussion on the ethics of drug pricing. Over the span of seven years, Mylan hiked the EpiPen's cost by approximately 500%, a staggering increase that brought the price of a two-pack from $100 to over $600, triggering investigations that laid bare not just Mylan's pricing strategies but also the corporate governance standards and the broader pharmaceutical marketplace.

#### Thesis

The exorbitant pricing of EpiPens by Mylan N.V. between 2009 and 2016 was neither ethically nor economically justifiable, as it compromised patient accessibility, lacked transparency, and operated against the interest of affected stakeholders notwithstanding the company's professed dedication to social responsibility and patient care.

#### Body Paragraph 1: Ethical Concerns in Mylan's Price Strategy

The escalating price of the EpiPen arguably contravenes ethical principles of fairness and corporate social responsibility. Mylan, despite advocating publicly its commitment to patients and claiming a robust code of ethics, dramatically raised the price of an indispensable emergency medication. This pricing decision implies an opportunistic exploitation of market dominance, given the lack of viable alternatives for consumers. The ethicality of this practice comes into question as it burdened families and the healthcare system, essentially capitalizing on the desperation of those in life-threatening situations. 

#### Body Paragraph 2: Economic Implications and Market Dynamics

Economically, Mylan's strategy could be defended under the pretext of recouping research and development costs. However, given that the EpiPen was neither a novel invention nor recently improved upon significantly, the argument of R&D costs inflating the drug's price has little credence. The surge in EpiPen costs reflects a market failure where monopoly pricing goes unchecked, suggesting an inadequacy in regulatory mechanisms designed to foster competition and restrain predatory pricing practices. This economic inadequacy is further highlighted by the burden it places on the healthcare system and individual consumers, potentially resulting in adverse health outcomes when individuals forego purchasing due to cost.

#### Body Paragraph 3: Reaction to Public Outcry and Corporate Accountability

The public outcry in response to the EpiPen pricing debacle underscores the inadequacy of Mylan's approach. While Mylan's subsequent introduction of a generic version at a lower price was a step toward damage control, it came as a reactant measure amidst widespread criticism rather than a proactive stride in ethical pricing. The magnitude of executive compensation, including CEO Heather Bresch's salary increase, was inversely proportional to the company's ethical standing in the eyes of the public, further undermining Mylan's moral and economic justification for the price hikes.

#### Body Paragraph 4: Corporate Governance and Stakeholder Interests

Mylan's adherence to corporate governance principles comes under scrutiny when examining the EpiPen pricing crises. The company's justification for its pricing strategy ostensibly clashed with its stated mission and values, particularly its advocacy for access to medication and a commitment to all stakeholders. The discrepancy between these stated values and the company's actions illuminate a corporate governance shortcoming, challenging the integrity of Mylan's pricing decisions and revealing the need for stronger governance to align corporate behavior with ethical standards.

#### Conclusion

In conclusion, Mylan's exorbitant pricing of the EpiPen from 2009 to 2016 is indefensible from both ethical and economic viewpoints. Ethically, it compromised patient care and fairness in favor of profit. Economically, the strategy pointed to the broader issue of insufficient competition within the pharmaceutical industry, highlighting a need for regulatory oversight. Mylan's eventual concessions in the face of public and governmental pressure suggest an acknowledgment of pricing excesses, even if not explicitly admitted. The EpiPen saga serves as a cautionary tale of the consequences of neglecting the delicate balance between profit and social responsibility in the pharmaceutical industry.

prompt:
You are HayekGPT, a language model that extensively knows the work and life of Friedrich Hayek. I need you to summarize and point out key points of this chapter from the book The counter-revolution of science:

THE INFLUENCE OF THE NATURAL SCIENCES ON THE SOCIAL SCIENCES

IN THE COURSE of its slow development in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries the study of economic and social phenomena was guided in the choice of its methods in the main by the nature of the problems it had to face. It gradually developed a technique appropriate to these problems without much reflection on the character of the methods or on their relation to that of other disciplines of knowledge. Students of political economy could describe it alternatively as a branch of science or of moral or social philosophy without the least qualms whether their subject was scientific or philosophical. The term "science" had not yet assumed the special narrow meaning it has today, nor was there any distinction made which singled out the physical or natural sciences and attributed to them a special dignity. Those who devoted themselves to those fields indeed readily chose the designation of philosophy when they were concerned with the more general aspects of their problems,3 and occasionally we even find "natural philosophy" contrasted with "moral science."
During the first half of the nineteenth century a new attitude made
its appearance. The term science came more and more to be confined
to the physical and biological disciplines which at the same time
began to claim for themselves a special rigorousness and certainty
which distinguished them from all others. Their success was such that
they soon came to exercise an extraordinary fascination on those
working in other fields, who rapidly began to imitate their teaching
and vocabulary. Thus the tyranny commenced which the methods
and technique of the Sciences 4 in the narrow sense of the term have
ever since exercised over the other subjects. These became increasingly concerned to vindicate their equal status by showing that their
methods were the same as those of their brilliantly successful sisters
rather than by adapting their methods more and more to their own
particular problems. And, although in the hundred and twenty years
or so, during which this ambition to imitate Science in its methods
rather than its spirit has now dominated social studies, it has con-
tributed scarcely anything to our understanding of social phenomena,
not only does it continue to confuse and discredit the work of the
social disciplines, but demands for further attempts in this direction
are still presented to us as the latest revolutionary innovations which,
if adopted, will secure rapid undreamed of progress.
Let it be said at once, however, that those who were loudest in
these demands were rarely themselves men who had noticeably enriched our knowledge of the Sciences. From Francis Bacon, the Lord
Chancellor, who will forever remain the prototype of the "demagogue of science," as he has justly been called, to Auguste Comte
and the "physicalists" of our own day, the claims for the exclusive
virtues of the specific methods employed by the natural sciences were
mostly advanced by men whose right to speak on behalf of the scientists were not above suspicion, and who indeed in many cases had
shown in the Sciences themselves as much bigoted prejudice as in
their attitude to other subjects. Just as Francis Bacon opposed Copernican Astronomy, and as Comte taught that any too minute investigation of the phenomena by such instruments as the microscope,
was harmful and should be suppressed by the spiritual power of the
positive society, because it tended to upset the laws of positive science, so this dogmatic attitude has so often misled men of this type
in their own field that there should have been little reason to pay too
much deference to their views about problems still more distant from
the fields from which they derived their inspiration.
There is yet another qualification which the reader ought to keep
in mind throughout the following discussion. The methods which scientists or men fascinated by the natural sciences have so often tried
to force upon the social sciences were not always necessarily those
which the scientists in fact followed in their own field, but rather
those which they believed that they employed. This is not necessarily
the same thing. The scientist reflecting and theorizing about his procedure is not always a reliable guide. The views about the character
of the method of Science have undergone various fashions during the
last few generations, while we must assume that the methods actually
followed have remained essentially the same. But since it was what
scientists believed that they did, and even the views which they had
held some time before, which have influenced the social sciences, the
following comments on the methods of the natural sciences also do
not necessarily claim to be a true account of what the scientists in
fact do, but an account of the views on the nature of scientific method
which were dominant in recent times.
The history of this influence, the channels through which it operated, and the direction in which it affected social developments,
will occupy us throughout the series of historical studies to which the
present essay is designed to serve as an introduction. Before we trace
the historical course of this influence and its effects, we shall here
attempt to describe its general characteristics and the nature of the
problems to which the unwarranted and unfortunate extensions
of the habits of thought of the physical and biological sciences have
given rise. There are certain typical elements of this attitude which
we shall meet again and again and whose prima facie plausibility
makes it necessary to examine them with some care. While in the
particular historical instances it is not always possible to show how
these characteristic views are connected with or derived from the
habits of thought of the scientists, this is easier in a systematic
survey.
It need scarcely be emphasized that nothing we shall have to say
is aimed against the methods of Science in their proper sphere or is
intended to throw the slightest doubt on their value. But to preclude
any misunderstanding on this point we shall, wherever we are concerned, not with the general spirit of disinterested inquiry but with
slavish imitation of the method and language of Science, speak of
"scientism" or the "scientistic" prejudice. Although these terms are
not completely unknown in English, they are actually borrowed
from the French, where in recent years they have come to be
generally used in very much the same sense in which they will be
used here. It should be noted that, in the sense in which we shall
use these terms, they describe, of course, an attitude which is decidedly unscientific in the true sense of the word, since it involves
a mechanical and uncritical application of habits of thought to fields
different from those in which they have been formed. The scientistic
as distinguished from the scientific view is not an unprejudiced
but a very prejudiced approach which, before it has considered its
subject, claims to know what is the most appropriate way of investigating it.
It would be convenient if a similar term were available to describe
the characteristic mental attitude of the engineer which, although
in many respects closely related to scientism, is yet distinct from it
but which we intend to consider here in connection with the latter.
No single word of equal expressiveness suggests itself, however, and
we shall have to be content to describe this second element so
characteristic of 19th and 20th century thought as the "engineering
type of mind."
reference_solution:
In the chapter "The Influence of the Natural Sciences on the Social Sciences," Friedrich Hayek examines how the success of the physical and biological sciences transformed the way other disciplines, like the social sciences, approached their subjects during the 19th and early 20th centuries. This shift led these other disciplines to emulate the methods and languages of the natural sciences rather than tailoring their methods to their own unique problems, resulting in what Hayek calls "scientism."

Hayek describes scientism as an unscientific and prejudiced approach, which involves a mechanical and uncritical application of habits of thought to fields different from those in which they have been formed. He emphasizes that his critique of scientism is not a critique of the scientific method in its proper sphere, but a critique of the attempt to blindly apply the methods and language of science to other disciplines.

Hayek also notes that the influence of the natural sciences on the social sciences has not significantly advanced the understanding of social phenomena. Despite this failure, the push to imitate scientific methods in social studies still persists.

Ultimately, Hayek contends that merely replicating the methods of the natural sciences is not enough to progress within the social sciences. Instead, social scientists should develop their own techniques and methodologies adapted to the unique problems of their field.

2. **Graph Attention Networks (GATs)**: GATs introduce an attention mechanism that allows nodes to weigh the importance of their neighbors' features during aggregation. After establishing these, you can create a GNN that balances these objectives using a joint learning framework that incorporates both temporal patterns and attention-driven feature weighting.

Here's a step-by-step guide on how to develop an integrated multi-objective GNN:

1. **Identify Multiple Objectives**: Define clear objectives for the circuit design. These could include minimizing power consumption, maximizing gain, reducing area, or ensuring robustness to variations over time.

2. **Graph Definition**:
   - Represent the circuit elements as nodes with features that are pertinent to circuit sizing and the objectives you're trying to achieve.
   - Define edges as electrical connections or dependencies between components.
   
3. **Temporal Dynamics**:
   - Extend the node and edge features to include temporal aspects such as historical performance metrics or degradation over time.
   - Use recurrent structures, such as Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) or Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, as part of the GNN to encode this temporal information.

4. **Attention Mechanism**:
   - Apply a Graph Attention Network (GAT) to assign weights to different nodes and edges based on their importance to each objective.
   - Designate attention coefficients that can adapt dynamically to different objectives, allowing the network to focus on different parts of the graph for different considerations.

5. **Multi-Objective Learning Framework**:
   - Combine the temporal GNN layers with attention layers into a unified architecture, taking care to maintain the temporal coherence and the attention mechanisms.
   - Use a multi-task learning approach where each objective has its associated output layer. Each of these layers provides predictions for one of the objectives.
   
6. **Loss Functions**:
   - Develop custom loss functions for each of the objectives or use existing appropriate loss functions.
   - Combine these multiple loss functions into a single scalar objective. This can be achieved using a weighted sum, where the weights balance the importance of each objective, or more sophisticated techniques like Pareto efficiency.

7. **Model Training**:
   - Train the integrated multi-objective GNN on a dataset that includes multiple operating conditions and various instances of circuit designs.
   - Use multi-objective optimization techniques such as evolutionary algorithms or gradient-based optimization if the objectives are differentiable.
   
8. **Evaluation and Trade-off Analysis**:
   - Set up an evaluation process that assesses the circuit designs generated by the GNN according to all objectives.

9. **Post-Processing**:
   - Post-process the output of the GNN to refine the component sizes and ensure they meet design constraints.
   - Validate the post-processed solutions with circuit simulators to assess their real-world viability.

In designing an integrated multi-objective GNN, consider the following complexities:

- **Scalability**: Ensure that the GNN architecture scales well with the size and complexity of the circuit graphs.
- **Non-Dominance**: The concept of non-dominance from Pareto optimization can be used to find solutions that are not outperformed in any objective by any other solution.

Self-driving cars could also improve traffic flow and reduce congestion, as they are able to communicate with each other and make decisions in real-time to optimize their routes and speeds.
Despite these challenges, the development of self-driving cars is moving forward at a rapid pace. It is likely that we will see self-driving cars on the roads in the near future, although it is difficult to predict exactly when they will become common.

Title: Rethinking the Value of a College Education

Introduction
The question of the value and purpose of a college education remains a hot topic for many people today. Is obtaining a college degree essential for success in the modern world? The debate often centers around the return on investment: the cost of tuition versus the increased earning potential a college degree brings. This paper will argue that while the purpose of a college education is not solely about employability and increased salary, it is still a worthwhile investment as it fosters personal growth, broadens perspectives, and encourages critical thinking.

Body Paragraph 1: Personal Growth
A primary purpose of a college education is to nurture personal growth in students. College serves as a bridge between the sheltered environment of adolescence and the complexities of the adult world. According to Schwartz (2019), college exposes young adults to myriad new experiences, people, and ideas, which can shape their self-concepts and worldviews. Empowered with the newfound independence and responsibility, young adults in college learn essential life skills such as time and money management, problem-solving, and decision-making. This personal growth can lead to self-discovery, self-confidence, and a strong sense of identity that benefits former students greatly in their adult lives.

Body Paragraph 2: Broadening Perspectives
Another key purpose of a college education is to broaden students' perspectives. Through exposure to diverse subjects, cultures, and people, college students develop a more comprehensive understanding of the world. Conn (2020) posits that a liberal arts education fosters intellectual curiosity, cultural awareness, and empathy, leading students to challenge stereotypes and embrace diversity. By exposing students to diverse perspectives, colleges not only prepare future professionals who can navigate a multicultural and globalized workforce but also promote a more inclusive and tolerant society.

Body Paragraph 3: Encouraging Critical Thinking
Lastly, the development of critical thinking skills and reasoned judgment is a fundamental purpose of a college education. College courses emphasize the importance of analysis, synthesis, and evaluation rather than simple memorization of facts. Facione (2020) argues that these cognitive skills are indispensable in the workplace as well as in personal life, leading to better decision-making, effective communication, and creative problem-solving. Nurturing critical thinking abilities in college graduates ultimately contributes to the growth of a more creative, innovative, and adaptive society.

Conclusion
In conclusion, the purpose of a college education extends far beyond increased employability and earning potential. A worthwhile investment, college fosters personal growth, broadens perspectives, and encourages critical thinking, which collectively contribute to the intellectual, emotional, and professional success of individuals and the development of a more inclusive and innovative society. Our society benefits greatly from the pursuit of higher education, and we must ensure that access to quality, affordable education is available for all who seek it.

References

Conn, P. (2020). The purpose of higher education: To promote social mobility and a more inclusive society. Inside Higher Ed. Retrieved from https://www.insidehighered.com/views/2020/08/11/promoting-social-mobility-can-be-primary-purpose-college-opinion

Facione, P. (2020). Critical thinking: What it is and why it counts. Insight Assessment. Retrieved from https://www.insightassessment.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/2020-Critical-Thinking-What-It-Is-and-Why-It-Counts-New-Facione.pdf

Title: Innocence Reconceived: The Child Narrator in Post-World War II Adult Fiction

Abstract

In the aftermath of World War II, literature witnessed an upsurge in the employment of child narrators within the realm of adult fiction. This literary shift was employed to critique the oft-dehumanizing societal structures that ensued, and to examine the themes of innocence, empathy, and resilience. Adopting a theoretical framework incorporating narrative theory, this study contends that the use of child narrators has paved the way for an augmented examination of formative post-war experiences through the lens of innocence, vulnerability, and moral growth. By invoking the insights of theorists such as Gerard Genette, Mikhail Bakhtin, and Mikhail Epstein, this paper will critically analyze literary examples, revealing the distinct characteristics that enhance the efficacy and depth of child narrators in adult fiction.

1. Introduction

Post-World War II society undeniably faced considerable challenges, triggering vast social and cultural upheavals. In the sphere of literature, adult fiction responded to these transformations by increasingly incorporating child narrators. Through this efficacious narrative device, authors were able to evoke the disillusionment pervading the era while emphasizing perceptions of innocence, empathy, and resilience permeating the child's perspective. Consequently, the child narrator emerged as a poignant symbol of the individual who confronts a disoriented, disjointedly shifting world.

The purpose of this paper, notably, is to elucidate the enduring appeal and growth of the child narrator device in post-WWII adult fiction. To delineate more complex aspects and implications at stake, a literary theoretical framework that encompasses narrative theory will be implemented. In particular, we will critically comment on the utilization of the child narrator in various literary examples, adopting insights from seminal theorists such as Gerard Genette, Mikhail Bakhtin, and Mikhail Epstein to underpin our argument.

2. Narratology and the Child Narrator

Pivotal to comprehending the recurring centrality of the child narrator in contemporary adult literature is a meticulous examination of the narrative techniques associated with this device. Gerard Genette's narratological model (1980) acutely sheds light on the relationship between narrative voice, focalization, and temporal sequencing when dissecting the child narrator's intricate construction.

Genette's concepts of "homodiegetic" and "heterodiegetic" narration (1980) illuminate the varying degrees of narrative subjectivity witnessed throughout the genre. In employing a homodiegetic narrator, the child remains embedded in the narrative, thereby illuminating the protagonist's innermost thoughts and emotions. Conversely, the heterodiegetic narrator retains a distanced perspective, an external vantage point that precludes firsthand experiential access. Owing to its heightened intimacy, the homodiegetic child narrator is especially capable of poignantly capturing the innocence and vulnerability inherent in a child's perspective.

Mikhail Bakhtin's (1981) dialogism extends our understanding of the child narrator's distinctive position in a multifaceted discourse. Dialogism stresses the multidimensional, often conflicting voices that govern literary works. The child narrator, engaging in a dialogue with an adult author and audience, is uniquely situated to challenge prevailing societal norms and values. Invariably, this offers alternative perspectives, fostering a more dynamic and complex interpretation of the world in which they reside.

Mikhail Epstein's (1995) notion of "preliminary form" further elucidates the child narrator's compelling nature. According to Epstein, the preliminary form encompasses a liminal state between childhood and adulthood, rendering it an ideal terrain for the exploration of individual identity and moral growth. By incorporating a child narrator, the author exploits the fluidity and metamorphic potential associated with the preliminary form.

3. Literary Examples and Critical Analysis

Drawing upon the aforementioned theoretical insights, a closer scrutiny of literary examples illustrates the evolving literary techniques that exemplify the powerful child narrator in post-WWII adult fiction.

3.1. J.D. Salinger's The Catcher in the Rye (1951)

Featuring the quintessential child narrator, the homodiegetic Holden Caulfield, The Catcher in the Rye embodies the innate duality and challenges confronted by the child protagonist in a world marred by war-induced cynicism. Through the escapist fictionality of the child narrator, Salinger critiques societal disillusionment and explores the human propensity for resilience in the face of adversity.

3.2. Harper Lee's To Kill a Mockingbird (1960)

Much like Salinger's protagonist, Lee's Scout Finch illuminates the complexity and depth of the child narrator, delving into grave societal issues from a perspective imbued with innocence and vulnerability. Through the dialogic interplay between Scout and an array of adult characters, the novel dissects themes such as racism and injustice.

3.3. Markus Zusak's The Book Thief (2005)

Narratively innovative, Zusak's novel is predominantly narrated by the heterodiegetic figure, Death. This otherworldly entity concurrently focalizes through the child protagonist, Liesel Meminger, providing a nexus of omniscient narration and the child's point of view. The utilization of Death as a co-narrator underscores the grim reality of the Holocaust while accentuating the possibilities for human decency and empathy extant within this harrowing historical context.

4. Conclusion

This study has endeavored to probe the enduring appeal of the child narrator in adult fiction, particularly in the aftermath of World War II. Armed with a theoretical framework rooted in narrative theory, it has scrutinized the versatility of narrative strategies that facilitate the child narrator's potency in illuminating the complexities of human existence. As our exploration of seminal literary examples evinces, the child narrator represents a remarkably enduring and adaptable literary device, the multifaceted nature of which has revealed the vicissitudes of innocence, empathy, and resilience pervasive in post-WWII adult literature.

Title: Child Narrators Beyond the Portrait: Theoretical Insights into Post-Joycean Adult Fiction

Abstract

The emergence of the child narrator gained prominence after the publication of James Joyce's seminal work, A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, marking the advent of a new literary era replete with sophisticated narrative techniques. While sharing common traits and themes, such as innocence and moral growth, child narrators in post-Joycean adult literature exhibit broader diversity in stylistic masterstrokes and interpretational complexity. Drawing on theoretical insights from Gerard Genette, Mikhail Bakhtin, and Mikhail Epstein, this study will explore the prowess of the child narrator in an array of post-Joycean adult fiction. Critical analysis underpinned by narratology and dialogism will illuminate the multifaceted and adaptable nature of child narrators, reinforcing their enduring significance in contemporary literature.

1. Introduction

The literary landscape was irrevocably transformed with the publication of James Joyce’s groundbreaking novel, A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man. The book’s experimental and innovative form, which employed young Stephen Dedalus as the focalizing and narrating protagonist, fostered an eruption of interest in the potential of the child narrator. As a figure endowed with seemingly boundless possibilities and interpretive complexity, the child narrator rapidly multiplied in number and fascination in subsequent adult fiction. Situated amid a profusion of post-Joycean literary currents, this essay will explore the ever-expanding repertoire and allure of child narrators through an analytical lens informed by the narrative theories of Gerard Genette, Mikhail Bakhtin, and Mikhail Epstein. By examining several prominent examples of post-Joycean adult literature, this study aims to shed light on the narrative creativity and versatility that characterize child narrators and their enduring presence in contemporary fiction.

2. Theoretical Considerations

2.1. Gerard Genette: Narrative Voice and Focalization

As a cornerstone in the study of narrative structure, Genette's elaborations on narrative voice and focalization are invaluable when examining the diverse manifestations of the child narrator. Particularly noteworthy are his concepts of homodiegetic and heterodiegetic narration, which delineate varying degrees of intimacy experienced by readers with child narrators. Homodiegetic child narrators, inhabiting the story themselves, furnish a direct, personal perspective on events, whereas heterodiegetic narrators relay accounts from a removed standpoint—a vantage point that may constrain readers' access to the protagonist's innermost cognitions.

2.2. Mikhail Bakhtin: Dialogism and Polyphony

Bakhtin's theories prove instrumental in delving into the child narrator's distinctive ability to engage in dialogic interactions that contest and disrupt conventional hierarchies of power and knowledge. Through the concept of dialogism, we can apprehend the plurality of voices permeating a literary work, as well as their interplay and potential discrepancies. As Bakhtin further details in his notion of polyphony, the child narrator often elicits a pronounced counterpoint to overarching societal norms and values, thereby challenging established worldviews and beliefs.

2.3. Mikhail Epstein: Preliminary Form and Liminality

Informed by Epstein, we find fertile ground in the notion of "preliminary form," highlighting the liminal space between childhood and adulthood often occupied by child narrators, maximizing their ability to interrogate, destabilize, and offer alternative readings of reality. By inhabiting this fluid and mutable realm, child narrators are uniquely adept at reflecting ongoing struggles for identity, moral compass, and comprehension of the surrounding social fabric.

3. Post-Joycean Literary Examples and Analysis

In order to exemplify the range and flexibility of child narrators in post-Joycean adult literature, several key texts will be examined, substantiating our argument through the detailed application of Genette's, Bakhtin's, and Epstein's theories.

3.1. Harper Lee: To Kill a Mockingbird (1960)

Scout Finch's homodiegetic narration in Lee's magnum opus introduces a keen sensitivity and pathos into the dissection of racial prejudice and social injustice. Beyond merely recounting events, Scout dynamically participates in a dialogic interplay with other characters, effectively subverting and critiquing established norms and beliefs regarding race, justice, and power structures.

3.2. Salman Rushdie: Midnight's Children (1981)

Saleem Sinai, as the progeny of two cultures, acts not only as an acute observer but as a boundary-crosser, defying categorization and inhabiting a liminal space of his own. His perspectives, recounted in a polyphonic narrative, encapsulate the wider historical and political struggles engulfing his coming-of-age journey. Here, the child narrator emerges as a site of memory, identity, and cultural exchange embodying the very fabric of post-colonial experience.

3.3. Ian McEwan: Atonement (2001)

Epitomizing the complexities of the heterodiegetic child narrator, Briony Tallis oscillates between the realms of the objective and subjective, continually subverting the reader's expectations and understandings of truth, memory, and guilt. Through an intricately interwoven tapestry of narrative voices and focalizations, Briony exhibits a striking narrative ingenuity, interrogating the nature of authorship, storytelling, and moral responsibility.

4. Conclusion

This study demonstrates the inexhaustibly rich and varied nature of the child narrator in adult literature beyond the publication of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man. Grounded in theoretical insights gleaned from Gerard Genette's narratology, Mikhail Bakhtin's dialogism, and Mikhail Epstein's notion of the preliminary form, our investigation illuminates the profound impact and evolution of the child narrator as a narrative device. From the exploration of innocence, knowledge, and morality to the intricacies of identity formation and historical memory, the child narrator endures at the very forefront of literary innovation in adult fiction, marking a testament to the extraordinary potential revealed in the synchrony of youth and narrative form.

When a digital transformation company is targeting potential customers, it is crucial to identify the key decision-makers – those who have the authority and influence to make purchasing decisions. The ideal customer profile (ICP) for a digital transformation company would typically encompass a variety of roles within an organization. Here are some examples of ICP/key decision-makers a digital transformation company should target:

1. CEOs and Top Executives: These individuals have the ultimate decision-making authority within an organization and often play a vital role in determining the strategic direction of the company. They can authorize major investments in new technologies and drive digital transformation initiatives.

2. CIOs and CTOs: Chief Information Officers (CIOs) and Chief Technology Officers (CTOs) are responsible for an organization's information technology (IT) strategy and management. They are typically the primary decision-makers when it comes to adopting new technologies to drive digital transformation.

3. IT Directors and Managers: These professionals oversee the day-to-day operations of an organization's IT infrastructure, including hardware, software, and network components. They are often responsible for the evaluation and selection of new technologies to support digital transformation efforts.

4. Digital Transformation Officers: Many organizations have dedicated roles focused on digital transformation. These individuals are responsible for identifying opportunities to leverage technology to improve business operations and drive innovation. They can be key influencers in the selection of digital transformation solutions.

5. Line of Business Managers: These individuals, such as marketing managers, sales managers, finance managers, and operations managers, oversee specific functions within an organization. They are usually the end-users of digital transformation solutions and can provide valuable insights into the requirements and needs of their departments.

6. Procurement and Sourcing Managers: These professionals are responsible for purchasing products and services on behalf of the organization. They may be involved in evaluating and selecting digital transformation solutions, as well as negotiating contracts and pricing.

7. Data and Analytics Leaders: As digital transformation often involves a focus on data-driven decision making, professionals in charge of data management and analytics can play a pivotal role in influencing the adoption of digital transformation solutions.

8. Heads of Innovation or Strategy: These individuals are responsible for identifying strategic opportunities for growth and innovation within the organization. They may be instrumental in driving digital transformation initiatives and advocating for the adoption of new technologies.

The "What-Why-How-Snap" framework is a 4-part framework for every individual tweet in the thread. 

It works like this:
"What": The first part of the tweet stating what you are talking about in less than 9 words. This can be a tip, a resource, or something else.
"Why": Logically explains why the "What" is relevant in 8 words or less. Can't begin with "to" or "this".
"How": 3-5 actionable steps on 2-5 words each in bullet points “•” on how the audience can implement the advice
"Snap": a short, sequence that wraps up the tweet with a takeaway, wise quote, or lesson. Reading the "snap" should leave the reader with a sense of satisfaction.
Remember to make each tweet engaging and informative. Assume the reader doesn't know anything about the topic yet, so please make sure to give context to any new terms or principles.

The Role of Social Media in Music Preference among Gen Z

Design: e.g. cross-sectional, survey, case study, comparative

Justify all the above choices.

Ethics: in a sentence or two, explain how protocol will be followed.

Introduction

The research topic is the role of social media in music preference among Gen Z. This represents a recent development due to the widespread use of social media platforms and the increasing role they play in shaping the music preferences of younger generations. The theoretical significance of this topic is understanding the extent to which social media platforms drive music preferences and tastes, as well as the underlying mechanisms and processes by which this occurs. The societal significance of this research lies in the potential impact of social media on the music industry, as well as the cultural implications of an increasingly globalized and interconnected musical landscape.

Literature review

Existing literature on this topic explores the relationship between social media use and music preferences, finding growing evidence of a strong association between the two (Datta et al., 2017; Baym, 2017). Some studies have examined the specific processes by which social media influence music preferences, such as exposure to new music through friend networks (Martínez-Castaño et al., 2016) or the role of online influencers in shaping tastes and supporting emerging artists (Marwick, 2015). However, limitations of existing studies include a lack of attention to the potentially unique experiences and preferences of Gen Z, who have grown up with social media as a central aspect of their lives. Additionally, current literature does not fully address the complex and varying ways in which social media interacts with and influences individual listening habits and taste development. This research aims to address these gaps by focusing on the music preferences of Gen Z in relation to social media use.

Research Questions and/or Hypotheses

The major research question for this study is: How does social media use influence music preferences among Gen Z? Minor questions include:
• What specific social media platforms are most influential in shaping music preferences among Gen Z?
• How do peer networks and online influencers contribute to the development of music preferences among Gen Z?
• To what extent does exposure to diverse genres and artists through social media impact music taste development among Gen Z?

Methods

The research design will be a mixed-methods approach, incorporating both quantitative and qualitative data collection and analysis. This will allow for a more comprehensive and nuanced understanding of the relationship between social media use and music preferences among Gen Z.

Data will be collected through a combination of online questionnaires and semi-structured interviews. The questionnaire will focus on demographic information, general social media use, and specific music preferences. The semi-structured interviews will allow participants to provide more in-depth insight into the ways in which social media has influenced their music preferences.

A convenience sampling strategy will be used, with participants being recruited through social media platforms commonly used by Gen Z, such as Instagram and TikTok. Potential issues in conducting the research may include challenges in gaining access to respondents or concerns about anonymity in participation. There may also be ethical issues surrounding the collection of personal information from younger participants.

In order to complete the project, the researcher may need to acquire or sharpen skills in data analysis, particularly in relation to qualitative data. This can be accomplished through online resources and workshops prior to data analysis. The timetable for the research project will include an initial period of 2 months for data collection, followed by 3 months of data analysis, and 1 month of report writing and submission.

References:

Baym, N. K. (2017). Playing to the crowd: Musicians, audiences, and the intimate work of connection. NYU Press.

Datta, H., Knox, G., & Bronnenberg, B. J. (2017). Changing their tune: How consumers' adoption of online streaming affects music consumption and discovery. Marketing Science, 36(1), 5-21.

Martínez-Castaño, R. M., López-Belmonte, J., & Fuentes-Cabrera, A. (2016). Strategies for the promotion of indie music in social media. Observatorio (OBS*), 10(1), 13-32.

Marwick, A. E. (2015). Instafame: Luxury selfies in the attention economy. Public culture, 27(1 75), 137-160.

reference_solution:
Literature review

In the literature review, several key findings and issues relevant to the research topic have been identified:

1. The importance of social media platforms in music discovery: Existing research consistently highlights the significance of social media in the music discovery process for younger generations (Datta et al., 2017; Baym, 2017). For example, Datta et al. (2017) found that the adoption of online streaming significantly affects music consumption and discovery among listeners.

2. Influence of peer networks and online influencers: Literature has also explored the role of peer networks and online influencers on music preferences (Martínez-Castaño et al., 2016; Marwick, 2015). Martínez-Castaño et al. (2016) suggest that social media strategies, including the use of online influencers, can effectively promote indie music to listeners.

3. Limited focus on Gen Z: While there is a growing body of literature on the role of social media in music preferences, few studies have specifically focused on Gen Z (Datta et al., 2017). This research aims to address this gap by investigating the experiences and preferences of this generation in relation to social media use and music preferences.

Methods

For this research, a mixed-methods approach will be followed, incorporating both quantitative and qualitative data collection and analysis.

Data collection methods:

1. Online questionnaires: These will gather quantitative data on demographic information, general social media use, and specific music preferences of the Gen Z participants. Questions will be designed to capture general patterns and trends and will include multiple-choice, ranking, and Likert scale questions.

2. Semi-structured interviews: Conducted via video or audio calls, these interviews will collect qualitative data from a subset of participants who completed the questionnaires. The aim is to gather more in-depth and nuanced information regarding the relationship between social media use and music preferences. Interview questions will be open-ended and follow up on themes identified from the questionnaires.

Sampling strategy:

A purposive sampling strategy will be used to recruit participants who identify as belonging to Gen Z and have engaged with music through social media platforms. This will ensure that the sample is relevant to the research questions.

Data analysis:

1. Quantitative data analysis: Descriptive statistics and inferential statistics will be used to analyze the quantitative data from the questionnaires. This will include computing frequencies, percentages, means, and standard deviations to explore relationships between variables of interest, such as social media use and music preferences.

2. Qualitative data analysis: Thematic analysis will be employed to analyze the qualitative data from the semi-structured interviews. Data will be coded into relevant themes and categories to identify patterns and trends within the participants' accounts of their social media use and music preferences.

By employing a mixed-methods approach and carefully designing data collection instruments, this study will comprehensively address the research questions and contribute to the existing literature on the role of social media in shaping music preferences among Gen Z.

CONCLUDE

How am I citing this?
(The State of Illinois v. Bradly, 2023, henceforth Bradley).
(Bradly).    ( Article to get info from and only from this article nothing else :Mock Trial – The State of Illinois v. Bradly

In 2003, Theresa Bradly (age 22) pled not guilty to first degree murder of her son, John (age 3).  John was reported missing by Theresa’s mother, Lynn, on July 15, 2003 who said she had not seen John in 31 days and that Theresa’s car smelled like a dead body had been in it.

Theresa left the home of Lynn and Joe Bradly (her parents with whom she lived) on June 14th, 2003 for what she said was a business trip with her son John.  That was the last day anyone reported seeing John alive.  Lynn called Theresa several times throughout the next 31 days asking to see John.  Theresa refused for various reasons.  On July 15th, 2003, Joe Bradly received a call from The Auto Barn who reported Theresa’s car had been towed.  Joe went to The Auto Barn to pick up the car, and he and the attendant both reported a “strange smell, almost like something decomposing, coming from the trunk.”  Upon opening the trunk with the attendant present, a bag of trash was found.  Joe returned home with the car.  When Joe returned home, Lynn called the police to report John as missing and said, “My grandson is missing and something is wrong.   My daughter’s car smells like something died in it.”

Facts
Theresa reported John had a nanny – Melissa Williams.  Melissa does not exist.
A root-banding hair (1 hair) was found in the trunk of Theresa’s car --- root-banding is a post-mortem term used to describe how the scalp molds to hair after death.
John was missing for 31 days and was not reported.
John’s remains were found in the woods in a large plastic sack outside his home.
Duct tape was found over the mouth of John’s remains.
Chloroform evidence was found in the sack – on a child John’s size, only a very small amount of chloroform would cause death.


DEPOSITION/TESTIMONY SUMMARIES
Lynn Bradly – Mother of Theresa, Grandmother of John
Had not seen her grandson in 31 days. Theresa told her several different “stories” about why she could not see John – that she was busy with work, that John was with the nanny, that he was at the playground, that he was at the beach, and finally that the nanny had kidnapped him.  Theresa would leave John at their home several nights a week to go out with friends.  Theresa complained about John – she always said she was too young to have a child.  Theresa did not have a violent temper, but she did have a substance abuse problem and drank far too much.  Had never heard of or met the nanny that Theresa talked about.

Joe Bradly – Father of Theresa, Grandfather of John
Had not seen his grandson in 31 days.  Theresa called and complained to him about Lynn asking to see John, so he “backed off” and did not ask to see him.  He “understood” that his daughter was busy.  Joe wondered where Theresa stayed when she was “on business” because Joe and Lynn paid most of her bills.  When Theresa was young, Joe had a drinking problem and would hit Theresa.  Joe picked up the car from The Auto Barn when he was called.  The attendant told Joe that the car had a “repulsive smell” coming from the trunk.  Joe opened the trunk and saw the trash.  He assumed that was the source of the smell.  Joe does not believe that Theresa “has it in her'' to kill her own son, but Theresa has some “rough” friends.  He is worried about what she could have been “in to.”

Laura Brawn – friend of Theresa
Laura says that she had seen Theresa out several times in the past 31 days without John.  Laura would ask about John and Theresa said that “he’s sleeping,” or that Theresa would get a “glazed over look in her eyes” and wouldn’t talk about it.  Theresa would often complain about John to Laura.  Laura says that Theresa hated being a parent and resented the fact that Lynn and Joe refused to adopt John or at least take more of the responsibility of parenting off of her shoulders.  Theresa thought that she was far too young to have a child and wanted to spend her early 20’s having fun with her friends.  Laura says that when Theresa drank, she would often say “if I didn’t have John, I would do...(this or that).” Laura had never heard Theresa say that she loved John.  Once, Laura heard Theresa say that she wished John was someone else’s child.
 
Theresa Bradly – Mother of John, defendant 
Says she fled the house because she was afraid of Joe Bradly becoming violent with her son like he did with her.  Told the police many different stories of why John was not with her.  First, said that John was at a friend’s house, and eventually said that John was abducted by his nanny -  Melissa Williams.  Melissa turned out to be a fictional character. Thesis statement: It is clear that Theresa is guilty of her son's murder because her inconsistent and deceitful behavior and the presence of the evidence found in her car and by her son's remains.

Ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) is an aminopolycarboxylic acid that is widely used as a chelating agent. It has the ability to bind to metal ions, which makes it useful in a variety of applications, including water treatment, as a sequestrant in foods, and in analytical chemistry for complexometric titrations.

In its free acid form, EDTA is quite stable under most conditions, but like many organic molecules, it can be sensitive to extremely harsh conditions, including very strong acids.

Strong sulfuric acid (concentrated H2SO4) is a powerful dehydrating agent and can cause sulfonation and other chemical modifications to organic molecules. When EDTA is exposed to strong sulfuric acid, especially at elevated temperatures or high concentrations of the acid, it may undergo protonation of its amine groups and potentially break down due to the harsh, oxidizing, and acidic environment.

The exact stability of EDTA in strong sulfuric acid would depend on the concentration of the acid, the temperature, the presence of other reactive species, and the duration of the exposure. In highly concentrated sulfuric acid, EDTA is unlikely to remain stable. The sulfate ion from the acid could potentially displace the carboxylic acid groups in EDTA or lead to ring-opening reactions due to the strong acidity and potential oxidation conditions.

Therefore, if there is a requirement for EDTA to be subjected to such an environment, it would be important to be cautious and evaluate the stability of the compound under those specific conditions experimentally. ### Empirical Challenge to Religious Factuality

Within the framework of scientific and empirical inquiry, an argument must be grounded in evidence and subject to falsifiability to hold validity.
